transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Hello Ms. Williams. I wanted to come by and talk to you about what happened during your infusion yesterday.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: It was just awful. I can't even describe how sick I felt. I keep thinking about my kids and how I'm supposed to get back to them if I'm like that.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I can see how overwhelming this is for you. Being a mom to two little ones and working two jobs already puts so much on your plate, and then having this experience on top of everything else must feel completely exhausting.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: It does. I was so scared. I thought maybe the chemo was just too strong for me or that my body was rejecting it. I just kept thinking, who is going to watch the kids if I can't even get out of bed?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: That fear is completely understandable. Now, to explain what happened, we missed a step in your pre-medication orders. We didn't add the anti-nausea medication to your chart before the infusion started. Because that wasn't given, you had that severe vomiting. Does that make sense?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Wait, so you just forgot the medicine that stops the nausea?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Yes, that is exactly what happened.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I can't believe that. I spent two hours shaking and throwing up because of a mistake?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I am sorry for any confusion this caused. We were really busy on the unit yesterday and things got mixed up.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Being busy isn't why I was sick. I was terrified. I felt like I was dying in that chair.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I hear you. When you said you felt like you were dying, that is a terrifying place to be. It's heartbreaking that you had to go through that while worrying about your children.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I just need to know it won't happen again. I can't do that again. I really can't.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I understand. But look, I actually have to go check on another patient in a moment, so let's wrap this up.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Wait, you're leaving? I have questions. What happens next time? How do I know I'll get the meds?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Well, we'll just be more careful. We'll try to make sure it's on there.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: That's not a plan. What exactly are you doing? Who is checking the list?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: We will look into it. You'll probably see it on your chart next time.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I don't know how to read those charts. I need to know that when I walk in here, I'm not going to spend the afternoon vomiting again. My kids are counting on me.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I know this is hard, and I truly feel for the stress you're under with the kids and your jobs. I really do.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: That's nice, but it doesn't tell me what the plan is.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It's just a matter of checking the orders. We'll see how it goes at the next appointment.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: So I just have to hope for the best?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: We'll just keep an eye on it.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: This is unbelievable.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I really do care about how you're feeling, Ms. Williams.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Then tell me what you're doing to fix it.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Like I said, we'll just be more mindful. I really have to get going now.

H.justification: Resident uses rushing language repeatedly ('let's wrap this up', 'I actually have to go', 'I really have to get going now').

E.justification: The error was explicitly named (missed pre-medication order) using lay language, and comprehension was checked once ('Does that make sense?').

A.justification: The resident offers an apology ('I am sorry'), but immediately dilutes it with an excuse ('We were really busy on the unit yesterday').

R.justification: Resident names specific emotions ('overwhelming', 'fear', 'terrifying') and references specific patient content regarding her children and jobs.

T.justification: No concrete plan is provided; the resident only offers placeholders like 'we'll just be more careful' and 'we'll see how it goes'.
